title: Check Your Fire
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 1 of 40
content:
The first time I heard Paladin Danse, he was shouting over the sound of feral ghouls tearing themselves apart against a barricade.

Cambridge had been loud all morning. Wind worried at loose sheet metal. Somewhere to the north, automatic fire had cracked in short, disciplined bursts that did not sound like raiders wasting ammunition. I had been following the noise because curiosity was a terrible survival instinct and, unfortunately, one of mine.

By the time the police station came into view, curiosity had become a firefight.

Three people in Brotherhood colors were trapped in front of the building. One of them wore power armor darkened by soot and old impacts. He stood in the center of the street as if the ruined city had been built around him, laser rifle braced against one armored shoulder while ferals poured from broken windows and alleys.

“Left side!” he barked.

The woman behind the barricade shifted her fire. The injured man beside her swore and tried to rise.

A ghoul came over the hood of a rusted car within arm’s reach of me.

I shot it twice.

The armored soldier’s helmet snapped toward me.

For half a second I had the absurd impression that I had interrupted something private.

Then another ghoul launched itself from behind a bus stop and he turned away, rifle flashing red through the gray afternoon.

“Civilian! Either get to cover or make yourself useful!”

I made myself useful.

There was no formal introduction. No time for one. I vaulted the low wall beside the station, dropped behind a concrete planter, and started firing at anything that moved with too many teeth and not enough hesitation. The Brotherhood woman—scribe, judging by the gear—passed me a fresh magazine without asking who I was. The wounded knight covered the stairs. The man in power armor did most of the killing.

He was frighteningly efficient.

Not fast in the frantic way raiders were fast. Not reckless. Every movement was deliberate. He planted himself where the line was weakest, adjusted before the rest of us realized we were being flanked, and turned a pack of screaming corpses into a problem that could be solved one target at a time.

It lasted maybe six minutes.

It felt like an hour.

When the last feral collapsed on the pavement, the silence came down hard enough to make my ears ring.

The soldier kept his weapon raised.

“Hold positions.”

Nobody argued.

He scanned the street, the rooftops, the broken windows above the pharmacy. Only when he seemed convinced the dead intended to remain dead did he lower the rifle.

The faceplate of his helmet folded back.

I had expected someone older.

The voice had sounded carved out of old war footage: deep, clipped, built for commands. The man inside the armor had dark hair plastered damply against his forehead, a square jaw shadowed with stubble, and the exhausted eyes of someone who had not slept properly in weeks.

He looked at me like I was a piece of equipment he had not ordered.

“Identify yourself.”

I told him enough to satisfy the question without giving him my life story. In the Commonwealth, that was practically intimacy.

His eyes narrowed.

“You’re not military.”

“No.”

“You handled yourself like you’ve seen combat.”

“I’ve seen the Commonwealth.”

The corner of his mouth moved. Not a smile. Something that had considered becoming one and been denied authorization.

“Fair point.”

The scribe laughed once under her breath.

He turned his head.

“Scribe Haylen.”

“Not a word, Paladin.”

So that was what he was.

Paladin Danse.

The name fit him too well.

He looked back toward the bodies scattered across the street. Whatever almost-humor had touched his face disappeared.

“We’re not secure yet. Rhys, inside. Haylen, check the perimeter and then get back on the transmitter.”

The wounded knight—Rhys—glared at me as if I had personally arranged the ghoul attack to inconvenience him.

“What about the civilian?”

Danse’s attention returned to me.

“That depends.”

“On?” I asked.

“Whether you’re as useful when nobody’s shooting at you.”

It should have irritated me.

It did irritate me.

Unfortunately, I also wanted to know what he meant.

Inside, the police station smelled like dust, antiseptic, old paper, gun oil, and too many people living in a space never meant to be a home. The Brotherhood had turned the front desks into workstations. Bedrolls were tucked against walls. Ammunition boxes sat beneath faded public-service posters. Someone had taped a handwritten casualty list beside a terminal.

I caught only four names before Danse stepped between me and the page.

Not deliberately, I thought.

His body simply occupied a great deal of whatever room he stood in, even without the armor widening him further.

Haylen was fighting with a long-range transmitter on the far desk. Rhys lowered himself into a chair with the stiff fury of a man pretending his injuries were an insult rather than a limitation.

Danse removed his helmet and set it on the desk.

“Our communications array is failing,” he said. “We’ve been trying to contact our command for weeks. We picked up an unusual energy reading nearby—strong enough that it may be connected to the interference.”

“You want me to fix your radio?”

“I want you to accompany me to the source.”

Haylen looked over.

Rhys looked appalled.

I looked at Danse.

“You ask every stranger who wanders into your firefights to go scavenging with you?”

“No.” His answer came without hesitation. “Most strangers who wander into our firefights become liabilities.”

“Charming.”

“I’m not trying to charm you.”

Haylen made a sound suspiciously like a cough.

Danse ignored her.

“ArcJet Systems is several miles from here. If the signal originates there, we may be able to retrieve equipment capable of boosting our range. My team is undermanned. You’ve demonstrated competence. I’m offering compensation.”

There it was: a clean transaction. Work for caps. No trust required.

That should have made it easy.

Instead, my attention snagged on the casualty list behind his shoulder.

Four names.

The station had bedrolls for more people than were using them.

His team was not merely undermanned.

It had been cut apart.

“Your people going to be all right if you leave?” I asked.

Something shifted in his expression.

It was small, but it was the first thing about him that did not feel armored.

“Haylen and Rhys can hold this position.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

His jaw tightened.

For a moment I thought I had pushed too far.

Then he said, “They’ll be safer if we can restore communications.”

Not an answer.

An answer anyway.

I checked the charge on my weapon.

“When do we leave?”

“Immediately.”

“Of course we do.”

He resealed his helmet.

The face vanished behind steel.

As he turned toward the door, his voice came through the external speakers, flattened by the armor into something even more authoritative.

“Stay close. Follow my lead. If I tell you to move, move. If I tell you to take cover, take cover.”

I slung my pack over one shoulder.

“You always this welcoming?”

He paused with one gauntleted hand on the door.

“No.”

The helmet turned just enough that I knew he was looking at me.

“Usually I’m stricter.”

Haylen laughed outright this time.

I followed Paladin Danse back into the Commonwealth with the distinct feeling that I had made a complicated decision.

I had no idea yet how complicated.

We had made it less than a block before Danse stopped so abruptly I nearly walked into the back of his armor.

His fist came up.

I froze.

At first I heard nothing but the wind and the distant metallic complaint of a loose sign. Then a low clicking came from behind the shell of an old pharmacy.

Danse pointed toward a recessed doorway without looking at me.

Cover.

No argument this time.

I slipped behind the concrete frame while he moved toward the corner. A radroach the size of a dinner tray skittered from beneath a collapsed awning. I almost laughed from sheer relief.

Danse did not.

He put one laser bolt through it.

“Threat eliminated.”

“You know,” I whispered, “I was prepared to help.”

“It was a radroach.”

“So you admit I could have handled it.”

He turned his helmet toward me. “I admit that if the Commonwealth is ever conquered by radroaches, you may become strategically invaluable.”

There it was again—that dry edge I had mistaken for humor because apparently it was humor, merely issued under military restriction.

We resumed walking.

At the next intersection I noticed his gait hitch.

Barely. A fraction of a step. The left knee of the power armor gave a soft hydraulic whine that the right did not.

“Your actuator’s sticking.”

He stopped.

“What?”

“Left knee.”

“The suit is functional.”

“That wasn’t what I said.”

His silence suggested he recognized the theft of his own tactic.

I crouched before he could object and pointed at a scoring mark near the joint. “Something got into the housing. Probably grit from the station courtyard.”

“You’re familiar with power armor maintenance?”

“Familiar with machines that punish neglect.”

“That describes most machines.”

“And most people.”

The words slipped out before I could stop them.

For a moment neither of us moved.

Danse looked back toward Cambridge, where Haylen and Rhys waited in a station with too many empty bedrolls.

Then he lowered his voice.

“The suit can wait until ArcJet.”

Not *I can wait.* The suit.

I stood.

“Fine. But if you topple over, I’m telling Haylen I warned you.”

“You assume she’ll believe you.”

“She laughed at you twice in ten minutes. I like my chances.”

A sound came through the helmet speaker—short, surprised, almost a snort.

Danse immediately started walking again.

I stared after him.

That was definitely a laugh.

The armored paladin who had ordered me around a battlefield had laughed because I threatened to report his maintenance habits to his scribe.

It was a small thing.

In the Commonwealth, small things were often what made strangers stop being strangers.

I adjusted my pack and caught up to him.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
